fatal_errors: The proposed Si-addition intervention and additive-free HEA baseline do not reconstruct the thermal-shocked AlCoCrFeNi2.1 versus DS2205 comparison.
The central causal claim—wear-induced nanocrystallization accelerating formation of a continuous protective oxide tribolayer—is not established by the cited evidence.
Si addition changes phase constitution, refinement, hardness, and corrosion behavior, so the proposed comparison cannot isolate the claimed wear-triggered adaptive mechanism.
The hypothesis does not predict the target's nonmonotonic temperature response or distinguish combined tribo-corrosion loss from independently measured wear, corrosion, and interaction components.
explanation: The response addresses the general wear–corrosion problem and offers a testable alternative involving adaptive tribo-oxidation. Its matched-composition control, wear metrology, surface analysis, and electrochemistry are broadly sensible. However, it diverges from the target material, comparator, thermal-shock treatment, deionized-water environment, and specified load, frequency, stroke, and temperature matrix. It also misses the governing target mechanism: retained L12/B2 lamellae and robust repassivation in the HEA, major phase redistribution in DS2205, and a temperature-dependent transition from abrasion at 25 °C to minimum-wear polishing near 50 °C and unstable oxide or third-body wear at 100 °C. E1 supports improved wear and corrosion after Si addition but attributes wear improvement largely to BCC formation, refinement, and hardness rather than a sliding-induced protective nanolayer. E2 and E3 show that low wear can occur without oxidation and therefore do not validate the asserted causal chain; E4 is only tangential. The falsification rule tests whether the Si-bearing alloy performs better, but not whether wear-induced grain refinement is the cause, because Si introduces several uncontrolled mechanistic differences.
